title: St Patrick (17 March)
hook: the breastplate prayer: Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me

segments.voice: Yesterday, three forties, each with a far side, and your line was forty is enough.

Green rivers, marching bands, a parade down the main street of cities nowhere near Ireland. That's one St Patrick's day. There's a quieter one, and it starts with a short piece of writing by the man himself. In it he doesn't sound like a hero. He sounds embarrassed. He says he was not a learned man, that he writes clumsily, that as a young man he didn't really know God. Then he tells how he was stolen from home, carried across the sea and made a slave in a strange country. The parade remembers a national saint. His own words remember a kidnapped boy.
screen: `A SHORT ACCOUNT BY THE MAN HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Patrick's own account is called his Confession. He grew up in Britain, in a Christian family, but says he paid its faith little attention. Raiders took him captive to Ireland, where he was set to watch flocks on the hillsides. And there, alone, cold and hungry, he began to pray, he says, day and night, in snow and frost and rain. After years of this, a voice in his sleep told him a ship was ready. He ran, found the ship, and got home. That should be the end. Instead he dreams of a man bringing letters, one headed the voice of the Irish, calling him, as he tells it, to come and walk among them again. And he goes back, to the country of his slavery, to spend his life there. Tradition gives Patrick a hymn called the Breastplate, a prayer you put on like armor before going out. Whether he wrote it is uncertain; it isn't in his Confession. But it sounds like someone who knows what it is to be alone in a hostile place. In one English version: Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ in me, Christ beneath me, Christ above me, Christ on my right, Christ on my left. Every direction covered; nowhere left empty. Some readers hear in it the shepherd boy on the hillside, finding out he was never alone. The shamrock and the snakes come later, from legend. The Confession is where the man himself speaks.
screen: `THE VOICE OF THE IRISH CALLS HIM BACK.`

segments.voice: Notice each direction of the Breastplate in turn: what's in front of you, behind, the ground beneath, the sky or ceiling above, your right, your left. If you pray, say the lines as you go, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ beside me; if not, notice you're held on every side, by the floor, the air, the room, and rest in the middle of it.
St Patrick. A boy taken as a slave to Ireland who escaped, then chose to go back, and whose name is tied to a prayer that fills every direction with Christ.
Your line: christ beside me. Before, behind, above, below. Day one thousand twenty-three, done.

howItsDone: Catholic and Anglican churches, and some others, keep St Patrick's feast with services and prayers, and the Breastplate is sung as a hymn or said as a morning prayer in some churches; in Ireland it is also a national holiday.

chat.says: Who was St Patrick, really? Isn't he just the shamrock and snakes guy?
options: In his own Confession, he's a kidnapped slave who escaped, then went back to Ireland.
He was an Irish chieftain's son who became a priest and never left home.
He was a Roman soldier sent to conquer Ireland, who converted on the way.
chat.meaning: Patrick's Confession tells of being taken as a slave to Ireland, escaping home, then going back. The shamrock and snakes came later, from legend.

Confession.meaning: Patrick's own short account of his life

Breastplate.meaning: a prayer tradition gives Patrick, put on like armor

shamrock.meaning: a three-leaved plant tied to Patrick by later legend

notes: Claims rule: Patrick's age at capture, the number of years in slavery, and dates are left out; 'after years of this' paraphrases the Confession's account (it gives six years). Confirm.
Breastplate lines are given as paraphrase 'in one common English version' (close to Kuno Meyer's and others) and not cited as a quotation; confirm wording is acceptable.
'Scholars aren't sure he wrote it' — the Lorica is generally dated later than Patrick; confirm phrasing.
The Confession's dream of Victoricus and the 'voice of the Irish' paraphrased; confirm.
Original is null: the sources are Latin/Old Irish and no single word fits.
